topic: software testing; fuzzing visualization; deep-learning mutation testing; JVM differential fuzzing
status: bounded cross-paper evaluation-design lead from three frame-sampled full texts plus a targeted later visualization-taxonomy check; not a claim that a universal proxy is invalid
claim: In this small cross-method sample, evidence sits at different levels and should not be conflated: FuzzSplore demonstrates an analyst-facing diagnostic interface but does not test analyst decisions or bug yield; PMT demonstrates more graded/stable mutation decisions in three DNN settings but does not calibrate them to field defects; JVM seed selection reports discrepancy yield and separately reports developer disposition for 25 bugs (21 confirmed or fixed). This supports a falsifiable evaluation question—whether intermediate signals predict deduplicated, developer-confirmed defects under matched compute—not a cross-field correlation estimate.
positive_evidence: FuzzSplore implements four linked views for target-specific AFL++ campaign inspection and explicitly recognizes limitations of coverage/bug-count proxies; its paper does not report a controlled analyst or bug-yield study.

PMT evaluates three model/dataset families and eight mutation operators, using posterior/effect estimates to address stochastic binary-kill instability; authors report sample-size/error/cost analyses.

JVM seed-selection study evaluates three JVMs and two fuzzers, counts unique inconsistencies, then manually investigates/submits candidate unknown bugs; it reports 25 developer-triaged reports, 21 marked confirmed or fixed.
A later TOSEM taxonomy derived 120 visualization analysis tasks from 33 fuzzing-practitioner interviews and maps existing tools, including FuzzSplore, to only a subset of those tasks.
counterevidence: The JVM study's 21/25 confirmed-or-fixed result shows that a carefully constructed differential-testing pipeline can yield substantial real-bug evidence; it is counterevidence to claiming all proxies are unvalidated.
FuzzSplore addresses campaign diagnosis for a specific target and does not claim to be a general bug predictor; absence of a user study in that paper is not evidence of ineffectiveness.
The later taxonomy measures task coverage, not users' accuracy, speed, satisfaction, or bug discovery; it cannot establish that visualization tools fail in practice.
The three papers use different domains, metrics, subjects, and budgets; they do not provide matched data from which predictive validity or a correlation can be calculated.

sources.title: Visualization Task Taxonomy to Understand the Fuzzing Internals
sources.sections: Official ACM abstract/results and tool-task map

falsifiable_test: On several fuzzing and DNN-testing targets, preregister a layered study that logs each method's intermediate metric (coverage, internal-stage/task evidence, mutation posterior, discrepancy), then runs equal total-compute campaigns and independently deduplicates, triages, and confirms bugs. Estimate calibration, precision/recall, ranking quality, and decision utility for confirmed defects, stratified by target and testing regime. Separately measure visualization users' task accuracy/time. The lead weakens if intermediate metrics reliably predict defect yield and downstream decisions across held-out targets, or if visualization adds no value over scalar reports. This batch did not run that experiment.
limitations: Only three sampled papers in one broad topic-period cell plus one abstract/results-level later task-taxonomy check. No common benchmark, denominator, matched budget, user study, or causal comparison across methods. No prevalence, novelty, or universal proxy-validity claim.

topic: deep neural network software testing; probabilistic mutation testing; mutation validity
status: bounded methodological lead from one sampled full text plus two abstract-level adjacent primary-source checks
claim: PMT addresses the repeatability of binary mutation-kill decisions under stochastic DNN training, but repeatability/graded posterior evidence is not the same as criterion validity: the sampled evaluation uses three model/dataset families and eight selected operators, reports empirical similarity-ratio thresholds, and does not show that its scores predict real deployed DNN faults. A 2024 real-fault-derived mutation pipeline for deep RL is relevant adjacent evidence, not a direct supervised-DNN replication; a 2025 report on monotonicity addresses the earlier DeepCrime criterion, not PMT itself.
positive_evidence: The PMT paper explicitly models variation across trained instances and reports a posterior-based approach, sample-size/error analyses, and approximately one minute per mutation after models are trained.
It evaluates MNIST, MovieLens, and UnityEyes model/dataset cases and eight operators, including source- and model-level mutations.

The authors themselves acknowledge that the empirical ratio scale is a practical heuristic, model/operator selection affects validity, and there is continuing debate over what counts as an acceptable DNN mutation.
muPRL derives operators from repository-mined real faults in deep reinforcement learning, showing that fault-grounded mutation design is a live, distinct axis of evaluation.
counterevidence: The three selected settings are diverse (classification, recommendation, synthesized eye-regression) and reuse prior artifacts to support replication; the study reports small approximation error at larger instance samples in those settings.

PMT may be applicable to other models/operators when trained instances are available; the authors describe a reusable implementation. Lack of real-fault calibration here is an evidence gap, not proof that the scores are uninformative.
muPRL concerns deep RL and has not been shown to transfer to the sampled supervised-DNN mutation operators.
The 2025 monotonicity report concerns DeepCrime's prior statistical criterion; it cannot be treated as proof that PMT has the same flaw or that PMT is superseded.

sources.title: muPRL: A Mutation Testing Pipeline for Deep Reinforcement Learning based on Real Faults
New Formulation of DNN Statistical Mutation Killing for Ensuring Monotonicity
sources.sections: arXiv technical-report abstract; concerns DeepCrime, not PMT

falsifiable_test: Mine and independently adjudicate real defects from multiple supervised-DNN repositories, preregister fault-derived mutations and train/test seed populations, then compare PMT posterior/similarity scores with real-fault detection at held-out repositories and fixed training/inference budgets. Report calibration, false positive/negative rates, ranking utility, robustness to threshold choice, and operator validity. The lead weakens if PMT predicts held-out real-fault detection across tasks with calibrated uncertainty; it strengthens if scores are repeatable but weakly related to real-defect detection. No such experiment was run here.
limitations: One PMT paper, three model/dataset cases, selected operators, and abstract-only checks of two adjacent sources; no replication, repository mining, or real-fault test performed. The observed scope does not prove PMT cannot generalize.

topic: software testing; JVM differential fuzzing; seed selection; corpus minimization
status: bounded empirical result from one full ICSE 2025 sampled paper; not independently reproduced
claim: For the paper's evaluated JVMs, two seed-driven fuzzers, and corpora, CFG-informed FISSCFG selection is a promising budgeted seed-reduction method: it reports 1.42–2.69× the full-set unique-inconsistency yield on benchmark corpora in the reported comparisons at low (about 30-second) extraction/selection overhead, and a separate new-bug experiment reports 25 developer-triaged bugs, 21 marked confirmed or fixed. This is not a universal best-method result: open-source programs add unique behavior, and alternative methods win some corpus/budget rows.
positive_evidence: The study evaluates 10 seed-selection approaches on HotSpot, OpenJ9, and Bisheng JDK with JavaTailor and VECT; inconsistency outcomes average five 24-hour experiments.

On its historical benchmark corpora, FISSCFG's selected subsets outperform FullSet in the reported budget rows by 1.42–2.69× unique inconsistencies; selection overhead for FISSCFG on P1 is reported as 30 seconds.
With a 50% FISSCFG budget, a separate RQ3 experiment reports 11 unknown bugs versus 5 for FullSet, with the paper's across-method bug tally at 25 total and 21 marked confirmed or fixed by developers.
The GitHub-derived P3 corpus contributes bugs not found by older benchmark corpora; seven of the confirmed-or-fixed reports were detectable only by P3.
counterevidence: Unique inconsistencies include potential real bugs, false positives, and duplicates; they are not interchangeable with confirmed bugs.
The paper's 21/25 label combines 'confirmed' and 'fixed'; it must not be reported as 21 fixed bugs.
Open-source corpus and pre-trained-model methods can contribute unique bugs and win particular rows, so seed choice is corpus/task dependent rather than universally ordered.
Only three JVM implementations, two fuzzers, selected corpora, and 24-hour runs were studied; authors note industrial fuzzing runs are longer and randomness matters.

sources.sections: Sections IV–VIII, Tables IV–IX, developer bug dispositions

falsifiable_test: Replicate across additional JVM implementations/fuzzers and diverse seed corpora while fixing total preprocessing plus fuzzing compute, include full-set, random, CFG, and corpus-mixture baselines, repeat with preregistered random seeds, deduplicate reports by root cause, and publish developer confirmation/fix status separately. Test whether CFG features improve confirmed unique bug yield on held-out JVMs. This batch did not reproduce the study.
limitations: One paper and no independent replication; potential imbalance in fuzzing time/preprocessing and the authors' bounded subjects/corpora remain relevant. Reported 1.42–2.69× is for unique inconsistency counts in selected benchmark comparisons, not an across-the-board real-bug multiplier.
